en: Dhammasaṅgaṇī 2:
Niddesa 2.4 Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa (The Section on the Commentary)
2.4.1. Extraction of the Meaning of the Triplets (Tika-atthuddhāra) 2.4.1.1.
The Triplet on the Wholesome (Kusalattika) Which phenomena are wholesome?
Wholesome states in the four planes—
these are wholesome phenomena.
Which phenomena are unwholesome?
The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness—
these phenomena are unwholesome.
Which phenomena are indeterminate?
Resultant states in the four planes, functional-undetermined states in the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are undetermined.
2.4.1.2. The Triplet on Feeling.
Which phenomena are associated with pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*)?
From the wholesome of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), there are four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by joy (*somanassa*); from the unwholesome, four;

and from the resultants and functional states of the sense-sphere wholesome, five; as well as the threefold and fourfold meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), both from the wholesome and from the resultant.
Excluding the feeling of pleasure arisen therein— the fourfold set of the functional, and the fourfold set of the supramundane jhānas, both wholesome and resultant—
these states are associated with pleasant feeling.
Which states are associated with painful feeling?
The two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure, and body-consciousness accompanied by pain— with the exception of the feeling of pain arisen therein—
these states are associated with painful feeling.
Which states are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
From wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), there are four types of mental arising accompanied by equanimity; from unwholesome consciousness, six;

from the result of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, ten; from the result of unwholesome consciousness, six; from functional consciousness, six; the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), both as wholesome and as result;
and the four formless-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) states, both as wholesome and as result.

The fourth supramundane jhāna, both as functional and as resultant, and the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising therein—excluding these—the remaining states are associated with the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. These are:
the three feelings, matter, and Nibbāna.
These states should not be said to be associated with pleasant feeling, nor associated with painful feeling, nor associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
2.4.1.3. The Triplet on Resultant.
Which states are resultants?
The result in the four planes:
these phenomena are results.
Which phenomena are of the nature to result?
In the four planes, the wholesome and the unwholesome—
these phenomena are phenomena that have the nature of ripening. Which phenomena are neither ripened nor having the nature of ripening?
In the three planes, the functional-indeterminate, matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are neither resultant nor subject to resultancy.
2.4.1.4. The Triplet on Clung-to (Upādinnattika).
Which phenomena are both acquired and subject to clinging?
The result in the three planes, and that form which arises from karma having been performed—
these phenomena are both acquired and subject to clinging.
Which phenomena are not acquired but are subject to clinging?

The wholesome in the three planes; the unwholesome; the functional-undetermined in the three planes; and that form which is not produced by karma—these phenomena are not acquired but are subject to clinging.
Which phenomena are not grasped and do not lead to grasping?
The four paths that are not included within the mundane world, the four fruits of asceticism, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are not grasped and do not lead to grasping.
2.4.1.5. The Triplet of the Corrupt (Saṅkiliṭṭhattika) Which phenomena are both corrupt and subject to corruption?
The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness.
These states are defiled and subject to defilement.
Which states are undefiled but subject to defilement?
Wholesome states in the three planes, resultant states in the three planes, functional-ineffective states in the three planes, and all form.
These phenomena are undefiled yet subject to defilement.
Which phenomena are undefiled and not subject to defilement?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are undefiled and non-defiling.
2.4.1.6. The Triad of Applied Thought:
Which phenomena are accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought?

The wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere; eleven types of consciousness arising as the result of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, two as the result of unwholesome consciousness, and eleven as functional;
the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere, both as wholesome and as result;
and the supramundane first jhāna, both as wholesome and as result—excluding the applied thought and sustained thought that arise therein.
These states are with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicārā*).
Which states are without applied thought and have only sustained thought (*avitakkavicāramattā*)?

In the fivefold system of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the second jhāna—whether wholesome (*kusala*), resultant (*vipāka*), or functional (*kiriya*)—and in the fivefold system of the supramundane (*lokuttara*), the second jhāna—whether wholesome or resultant—excluding the sustained thought (*vicāra*) arisen therein, as well as applied thought (*vitakka*).
These states are without applied thought and have only sustained thought.
Which states are without applied thought and without sustained thought?
The two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, and the fine-material-sphere first jhāna—whether wholesome, resultant, or functional.

The four formless attainments (āruppa), whether as wholesome, resultant, or functional; the nine supramundane jhānas (lokuttara-jhāna) according to the threefold system, whether as wholesome or resultant;

the second jhāna in the fivefold system; and the arisen sustained thought (vicāra), as well as material form (rūpa) and Nibbāna—these states are without initial application and without sustained application (avitakka-avicāra).

Investigation (vicāra) arising together with applied thought (vitakka) should not be called "with applied thought and sustained thought" (savitakkasavicāra), nor "without applied thought and with sustained thought only" (avitakkavicāramatta), nor "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (avitakka-avicāra).
2.4.1.7. The Triplet on Rapture (Pītttika) Which phenomena are accompanied by rapture (pīti)?
From the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere, there are four types of consciousness arising together with joy; from the unwholesome, four;
from the resultants of the wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, five; from the functional, five;

from the wholesome, resultant, and functional jhānas of the fine-material sphere belonging to the two sets of three; and from the wholesome and resultant jhānas of the supramundane—excluding the joy arisen therein.
These states are accompanied by rapture (*pīti*).
Which states are accompanied by pleasure (*sukha*)?

From the wholesome of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), there are four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by joy (*somanassa*); from the unwholesome, four; and from the wholesome of the sense sphere...
Six [kinds of consciousness] from the resultant, five from the functional, the threefold and fourfold jhānas of the fine-material sphere from the wholesome,
resultant, and functional, and the threefold and fourfold jhānas of the supramundane from the wholesome and resultant— with the exception of the pleasure arisen therein—
these states are accompanied by pleasure.
Which states are accompanied by equanimity?
From wholesome states of the sense sphere, there are four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by equanimity; from unwholesome states, six;
from the resultants of wholesome sense-sphere states, ten; from the resultants of unwholesome states, six; from functional states, six; and the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere.
The wholesome, the resultant, and the functional [states] of the four formless attainments;
the wholesome and the resultant of the supramundane fourth jhāna— excluding the equanimity arisen therein—
these states are accompanied by equanimity.
Rapture is not accompanied by rapture; it is accompanied by pleasure, not accompanied by equanimity.
Pleasure is not accompanied by pleasure; it may be accompanied by rapture, not accompanied by equanimity, or it may not be said to be accompanied by rapture.
There are two types of consciousness-arising accompanied by mental grief, body-consciousness accompanied by pain, whatever feeling is equanimity, and both form and Nibbāna.
These states are not to be described as accompanied by rapture, nor as accompanied by pleasure, nor as accompanied by equanimity.
2.4.1.8. The Triplet of What is to be Abandoned by Seeing:
Which states are to be abandoned by seeing?
The four types of consciousness-arising associated with views, and the consciousness-arising accompanied by doubt—
these states are to be abandoned by vision.
Which states are to be abandoned by cultivation?
A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness—
these states are to be abandoned by cultivation.
The four types of greed-accompanied states of consciousness dissociated from views, and the two types of grief-accompanied states of consciousness—
These phenomena may be abandoned by vision, or they may be abandoned by cultivation.
Which phenomena are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation?
The wholesome in the four planes, the resultants in the four planes, the functional-undetermined in the three planes, and both form and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
2.4.1.9. The Triplet on Roots to be Abandoned by Vision:
Which phenomena have roots that are to be abandoned by vision?
The four types of consciousness associated with views, and the type of consciousness accompanied by doubt— excluding the delusion that has arisen therein—
these states have roots to be abandoned by vision.
Which states have roots to be abandoned by cultivation?
A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness— excluding the delusion arisen therein—
these are the states whose roots are to be abandoned by cultivation.
There are four types of greed-accompanied states of consciousness dissociated from views, and two types of grief-accompanied states of consciousness.
These states may have roots that are to be abandoned by vision, or they may have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Which states have roots that are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation?

Delusion accompanied by doubt, delusion accompanied by restlessness, the wholesome in the four planes, the resultants in the four planes, the functional-inindeterminate in the three planes, and both form and Nibbāna.
These states have roots that are to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.
2.4.1.10. The Set of Leading to Accumulation:
Which states lead to accumulation?
Wholesome states and unwholesome states in the three planes—
these are the states that lead to accumulation.
Which states lead to diminution?
The four paths that are not included [within the realms]—
these states lead to non-accumulation.
Which states lead neither to accumulation nor to non-accumulation?
In the four planes, resultant [states]; in the three planes, functional-indeterminate states, matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena neither lead to accumulation nor lead to dispersal.
2.4.1.11. The Triplet on the Trainee (Sekkhattika).
Which phenomena are those of the trainee (sekkha)?
The four paths not included [in the mundane world], and the first three fruits of recluseship—
these phenomena are those of the trainee.
Which phenomena are those of one beyond training (asekkha)?
The fruit of arhatship, which is the highest state—
these phenomena are those of one beyond training.
Which phenomena are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
The wholesome in the three planes, the unwholesome, the resultant in the three planes, the functional-indeterminate in the three planes, and both form and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
2.4.1.12. The Triplet of the Limited (Parittattika) Which phenomena are limited (paritta)?
Wholesome states of the sense sphere, unwholesome states, all resultants of the sense sphere, the indeterminate functional states of the sense sphere, and all matter.
These states are limited.
Which states are sublime?
Those pertaining to the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere, whether wholesome or indeterminate.
These states are sublime.
Which states are immeasurable?
The four paths that are not included [in the mundane world], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are immeasurable.
2.4.1.13. The Triplet of Limited Objects:
Which phenomena have limited objects?
All resultant states of the sense sphere, the functional mind-element, and the functional mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy—
these states have limited objects.
Which states have exalted objects?
The base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
these states have a sublime object.
Which states have an immeasurable object?
The four paths that are not included within the mundane realms, and the four fruits of recluseship—these states have an immeasurable object.

From the wholesome states of the sense-sphere, there are four types of consciousness-arising dissociated from knowledge; from the functional states, there are four types of consciousness-arising dissociated from knowledge; and all unwholesome states.

These states may have limited objects, may have exalted objects, but do not have immeasurable objects; they may also not be described as having limited objects, nor as having exalted objects. They consist of:
four types of wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge arising in the sense sphere; four types of functional consciousness associated with knowledge arising in the sense sphere;
the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, both wholesome and functional; and the functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and rooted in kamma.
These states may have limited objects, may have exalted objects, may have immeasurable objects, or may not be described as having limited objects, exalted objects, or immeasurable objects.
The fine-material-sphere triplets and fourfold jhānas— whether wholesome, resultant, or functional— the result of the fourth jhāna, the base of infinite space, and the base of nothingness—
these states are not to be described as having limited objects, exalted objects, or immeasurable objects.
Form and Nibbāna are without an object.
2.4.1.14. The Low Triplet:
Which phenomena are low?
The twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising—
these phenomena are inferior.
Which phenomena are mediocre?
Wholesome states in the three planes, resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all form—
these phenomena are middling.
Which phenomena are sublime?
The four paths that are not included [within the realms], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are sublime.
2.4.1.15. The Triplet on Wrongness-Entailing Certainty.
Which states are fixed in the wrong way?
The four types of consciousness associated with views and the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure—
these states may be fixed in the wrong way, or they may be unfixed.
Which phenomena are fixed in the rightness [of liberation]?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane]—
these phenomena are fixed in the rightness [of liberation].
Which states are indeterminate?
The four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by greed but dissociated from views; consciousness-arising accompanied by doubt;
consciousness-arising accompanied by restlessness; wholesome states in the three planes; resultant states in the four planes; and wholesome states in the three planes.
Functional indeterminate states, matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are undetermined.
2.4.1.16. The Triplet on Having the Path as Object.
Which states have the Path as their object?

The four types of consciousness-arising associated with knowledge from wholesome states of the sense sphere, and the four types of consciousness-arising associated with knowledge from functional states—
these states may have the Path as their object, but they do not have the Path as their cause.
They may have the Path as their dominant factor, or they may not be said to have the Path as their object, nor to have the Path as their dominant factor.
The four noble paths do not have the Path as their object; they have the Path as their cause;
they may have the Path as their dominant factor, or they may not be said to have the Path as their dominant factor.
The fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), both wholesome and functional, and the mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and associated with functional roots—
these states may have the Path as their object;
they do not have the Path as their cause, nor do they have the Path as their predominance.
It may not be said that they have the Path as their object.
[These consist of: the four types of consciousness-arising dissociated from knowledge from wholesome states of the sense-sphere; all unwholesome states; all resultants of the sense-sphere;
six types of consciousness-arising from the functional; and the threefold and fourfold jhānas of the fine-material sphere from both the wholesome and the resultant.
The result of the fourth jhāna; the four formless attainments (āruppa) as wholesome, as result, and as functional (kiriya);

and the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala)—these states should not be said to have the Path as their object (maggārammaṇa), nor to have the Path as their cause (maggahetuka), nor to have the Path as their predominance (maggādhipati).
Form and Nibbāna are without an object.
2.4.1.17. Triplet on the Arisen:
Which phenomena are arisen?
The result in the four planes and whatever form arises from the performance of kamma—
these phenomena may be arisen or may be subject to arising;
they should not be said to be unarisen.
Wholesome states in the four planes, unwholesome states, functional-undetermined states in the three planes, and that form which is not produced by past action—
these phenomena may be arisen, may be unarisen, but they should not be said to be "bound to arise.
Nibbāna should not be said to be arisen, nor unarisen, nor bound to arise.
2.4.1.18. The Triplet of the Past:
(…. With the exception of Nibbāna, all phenomena may be past, may be future, or may be present.
Nibbāna should not be said to be past, nor future, nor present.
2.4.1.19. The Triplet on Past Objects.
Which states have past objects?
The base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These states have the past as their object.
There are none that necessarily have the future as their object.
Which states have the present as their object?
The two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses and the three mind-elements—these states have present objects.

There are ten types of consciousness arising from the result of wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere; from the result of unwholesome kamma, the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity; and the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy.
These states may have the past as their object, may have the future as their object, or may have the present as their object.
The nine types of consciousness arising from sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and functional states, and the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere from both the wholesome and the functional—
these states may have the past as their object, may have the future as their object, or may have the present as their object.
It may not be said that they have a past object, nor that they have a future object, nor that they have a present object.
The fine-material-sphere triplets and fourfold jhānas— whether wholesome, resultant, or functional— the result of the fourth jhāna,
the base of infinite space, the base of nothingness, the four unconditioned paths, and the four fruits of recluseship— [are so].
These states should not be said to have a past object, nor a future object, nor a present object.
Matter and Nibbāna are without objects.
2.4.1.20. The Triplet on the Internal.
Excluding matter not bound to the faculties and Nibbāna, all phenomena may be internal, may be external, or may be both internal and external.
Matter not bound to the faculties and Nibbāna are external.
2.4.1.21. The Triplet of Internal Objects.
Which phenomena have internal objects?
The base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
these phenomena have internal objects.
Which states have external objects?

The threefold and fourfold jhānas of the fine-material sphere, whether wholesome, resultant, or functional; the resultant of the fourth jhāna; the base of infinite space; the four supramundane paths and the four fruits of recluseship—these states have external objects.
Excluding form, all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), as well as the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*)—

both wholesome and functional— these states may have an internal object, may have an external object, or may have both an internal and external object. The base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) should not be said to have an internal object, nor an external object, nor an internal-and-external object.
Form and Nibbāna are without an object.
2.4.1.22. The Triplet on the Visible with Resistance:
Which phenomena are visible and impinging?
The visible base—
these phenomena are visible and impinging.
Which phenomena are invisible and impinging?
The eye-base …pe… the tangible-object-base—
these phenomena are non-demonstrable and impinging.
Which phenomena are non-demonstrable and non-impinging?

Wholesome states in the four planes; unwholesome states in the four planes; resultant states in the four planes; functional-undetermined states in the three planes; and whatever form is non-demonstrable and non-reactive, included within the base of mental phenomena, as well as Nibbāna—these states are non-demonstrable and non-reactive.
This concludes the triad.
